Transitioning to Remote-First Team Structure

teamremote-workcultureprocess

Context

Post-pandemic, our team was split between office and remote workers. The hybrid model created two classes of employees and made collaboration inconsistent. We needed to decide on a deliberate approach.

Decision

Adopt a remote-first model where all meetings and collaboration assume remote participation, with optional office space for those who prefer it

Alternatives Considered

Return to office-first

Pros
  • Easier spontaneous collaboration
  • Clearer work-life boundaries
  • Existing office infrastructure
Cons
  • Limits hiring to local candidates
  • Some team members strongly prefer remote
  • Commute time reduces productivity

Hybrid with required office days

Pros
  • Balance of remote and in-person
  • Maintains some office culture
Cons
  • Creates two-tier experience
  • Remote workers miss hallway conversations
  • Scheduling complexity

Remote-first with optional office

Pros
  • Equal experience for all team members
  • Access to global talent pool
  • Flexibility for individual preferences
Cons
  • Requires intentional culture building
  • Harder to onboard new team members
  • Risk of isolation

Reasoning

Remote-first ensures everyone has the same experience regardless of location. This levels the playing field and allows us to hire the best talent regardless of geography. The key is being intentional about communication and culture rather than relying on office proximity.

The Hybrid Problem

Our hybrid setup had issues:

  • Office workers had context from hallway conversations
  • Remote workers felt like second-class citizens
  • Meetings were awkward (half in room, half on screen)
  • Documentation was inconsistent (office folks just asked each other)

Remote-First Principles

We established core principles:

1. Default to Async

  • Decisions documented in writing
  • Meetings have agendas and notes
  • No “you had to be there” moments

2. Over-Communicate

  • Daily standups in Slack (async)
  • Weekly team syncs (video)
  • Monthly all-hands with recordings

3. Intentional Synchronous Time

  • Pair programming sessions
  • Brainstorming calls
  • 1:1s remain synchronous

4. Document Everything

  • ADRs for technical decisions
  • Runbooks for operations
  • Onboarding guides maintained

Implementation

Tooling upgrades:

  • Invested in good video conferencing
  • Adopted Notion for documentation
  • Slack channels for team communication
  • Loom for async video updates

Process changes:

  • All meetings have video links (even if some are in office)
  • Meeting notes required within 24 hours
  • “No meeting Wednesdays” for deep work

Culture building:

  • Virtual coffee chats (random pairing)
  • Quarterly in-person offsites
  • Slack channels for non-work interests

Results After 6 Months

  • Hiring: Expanded candidate pool significantly
  • Documentation: 3x more written docs than before
  • Meeting efficiency: Meetings shorter and more focused
  • Team satisfaction: Survey scores improved

Challenges

  • Onboarding: New hires need more structured support
  • Isolation: Some team members struggle with remote work
  • Time zones: Global team means async by necessity

Remote-first isn’t perfect, but it’s more equitable than hybrid and gives us access to talent we couldn’t reach before.
